newsitem.title: FRANCE: Le Pen vows to sue French accusers on Jewish slur.
newsitem.headline: Le Pen vows to sue French accusers on Jewish slur.

text.p: French extreme-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, saying he was victim of a plot to turn Jews against him, denied on Tuesday ever saying President Jacques Chirac was in the pay of Jewish organisations.
"Once again, words I never said are attributed to me and the whole of the political and media world uses them to launch a witchhunt against me," Le Pen said in a statement.

Le Pen, whose National Front won control of a fourth town last month, is quoted in a new book as saying Chirac was "in the grasp...of Jewish organisations and notably the notorious B'nai Brith," a U.S.-based Jewish masonic welfare organisation.
Le Pen said he had a tape recording of the interview with the authors of "Le Roman d'un President" (A President's Story) which proved he spoke "in very moderate terms" of B'nai Brith.

He said he would sue the authors, journalists Nicholas Domenach and Maurice Szafran, and denied derogatory comments they attributed to him about Jacques Friedmann, a close friend of Chirac, and former minister Michele Barzach, both Jews.
Le Pen said the reported remarks, released last Friday ahead of publication this week, were deliberately made public on the eve of a meeting between Chirac and French Jewish leaders.
The reported comments raised a barrage of criticism and calls for the anti-immigration crusader to be put on trial.
Justice Ministry sources said before Le Pen's statement they were investigating the possibility of legal action but that it seemed unlikely he had broken the law.

Le Pen won 15 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential election. While France's far-right press regularly fulminates against what it sees as a conspiracy of Jews and freemasons, Le Pen has usually been more guarded since a series of explosive statements in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
